PigeonholeWheel

one pigeon per wheel
Proof drafted, not yet builtring 1Foundations: wheels, cycles and columns

When a new wheel joins, each position that survived the earlier wheels has one copy in the longer cycle for every slot of the new wheel. No two copies share a slot, so by the pigeonhole principle every slot receives exactly one copy: one copy is closed and the others, one fewer than the wheel size, stay open. Starting from the two open positions of wheels 2 and 3 (the 6n+1 and 6n-1 positions), two survivors are carried through every further wheel; if every prime were a wheel, only position 1 would be open, so the primes never run out. The per-wheel statement is the Chinese Remainder Theorem seen one wheel at a time; the infinitude proof is a known variant of Euclid's, related to the proofs through Euler's totient function.

What it adds: A third proof that the primes never run out, next to the two in Infinitude: it builds no special number (Euclid) and counts no square-free parts, but follows the wheels one at a time, showing by pigeonhole that each new wheel closes exactly one copy of every survivor and leaves the rest open.

Published sources

  • Euclid, Elements, Book IX, Proposition 20 (D. E. Joyce's edition) — the theorem proved; this node's argument is a counting variant of Euclid's
  • R. Meštrović, Euclid's theorem on the infinitude of primes: a historical survey of its proofs (300 B.C.-2022) — surveys the published proofs, including those through Euler's totient function, to which this survivor-counting proof is related
  • Chinese remainder theorem (Wikipedia) — the per-wheel statement is the Chinese Remainder Theorem for one new modulus, proved here by pigeonhole

Claims (4)

one_closed_copy
proof drafted, not yet built
For a new wheel not dividing the product of the earlier wheels, exactly one copy of any position lands on the blocked slot.
/-- **One pigeon per wheel.** For a new wheel whose size `q` does not divide
the product `M` of the earlier wheels, exactly one copy of any position lands
on the blocked slot. -/
def one_closed_copy : Prop :=
  ∀ q M start : Nat, q.Prime → ¬ q ∣ M → ∃! i : Fin q, lift_slot q M start i = 0
Rests on: no other node (Mathlib and the Vocabulary only)

open_copies
proof drafted, not yet built
The copies left open on the new wheel number exactly one fewer than the wheel size.
/-- **The holes.** Under the same conditions, the copies left open number
exactly one fewer than the wheel size. -/
def open_copies : Prop :=
  ∀ q M start : Nat, q.Prime → ¬ q ∣ M →
    (Finset.univ.filter (fun i : Fin q => lift_slot q M start i ≠ 0)).card = q - 1
Rests on: no other node (Mathlib and the Vocabulary only)

two_survivors_persist
proof drafted, not yet built
For any wheels of size at least 5, the cycle of 6 times their product has two different positions open on every wheel, including 2 and 3.
/-- **Two survivors persist.** For any set `W` of wheels of size at least 5,
the cycle of length 6 times the product of `W` has two different positions
open on the wheels 2, 3 and every wheel in `W`. -/
def two_survivors_persist : Prop :=
  ∀ W : Finset Nat, (∀ q ∈ W, q.Prime ∧ 5 ≤ q) →
    ∃ x y, x < 6 * ∏ p ∈ W, p ∧ y < 6 * ∏ p ∈ W, p ∧ x ≠ y ∧
      survives W x ∧ survives W y
Rests on: no other node (Mathlib and the Vocabulary only)

pigeonhole_primes_unbounded
proof drafted, not yet built
Above every bound there is a prime: two survivors cannot both sit on the one safe position.
/-- **Infinitude by pigeonhole.** Above every bound there is a prime: if every
prime were below the bound, every position other than 1 would be closed, yet
two different positions survive. -/
def pigeonhole_primes_unbounded : Prop :=
  ∀ limit : Nat, ∃ p, p.Prime ∧ limit ≤ p
